```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6,
```

```{r setup}
library(multiDetectR)
```

This vignette applies the allocation rule to a real **two-level** freshwater
environmental DNA (eDNA) survey of the fish community in Burns Harbor on Lake
Michigan, sampled by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service in 2023 and 2024.
As in the marine vignette, the model-fitting is done by the reproducible
`targets` pipeline in `data-raw/analysis/carp/` of this package; here we take the
pipeline's fitted per-level detectabilities and feed them to `allocate()`.
The numbers below are copied from the pipeline outputs so the vignette builds
without the field data.

## Two levels, not three

Unlike the marine survey, the freshwater survey has only two levels:

1. **sites** (the outermost, reporting level; occupancy `psi`), and
2. **water samples** within a site (per-sample detection `p`).

Only a few samples carried molecular replicates, so the design does not support
a third (replicate) level.
A two-level occupancy model (fit with `occStan` in the pipeline) estimates `psi`
and `p` for each species.
The table below gives the median estimates for three species of management
interest, taken from the pipeline output `data/all_summary.csv`.

```{r theta}
## Median per-level detectabilities from the two-level occupancy fits
## (pipeline output all_summary.csv); psi = site, p = per-sample detection.
fresh_theta <- data.frame(
  species = c("Cyprinus carpio", "Dorosoma cepedianum",
              "Neogobius melanostomus"),
  psi     = c(0.743, 0.744, 0.749),
  p       = c(0.710, 0.714, 0.809)
)
fresh_theta
```

These three carry unusually high per-sample detection; most species in the
assemblage had much lower, more uncertain detection, which is why the survey
leans on visiting many sites rather than deep sampling within a site.

## Per-level costs

A two-level freshwater design prices a site and a water sample.
We use the same site and sample unit costs as the marine example for
comparability (a site visit and a filtered water sample are the cost drivers);
there is no replicate level to price here.

```{r cost}
fresh_cost <- c(site = 100, sample = 100)
```

## Allocating a budget for one species

Take the first species and ask how a \$3,000 budget should be split between
sites and samples to best detect it where it is present.

```{r allocate}
theta_one <- unlist(fresh_theta[1, c("psi", "p")])
theta_one

design <- allocate(
  theta  = theta_one,
  cost   = fresh_cost,
  goal   = "detection",
  budget = 3000
)
design
summary(design)
```

With only two levels and a site and a sample costing the same, the rule has
little room to shift effort inward: the design is close to the naive one, which
is the rule's own lesson that optimizing barely matters at shallow depth.
The payoff of the allocation rule grows with the number of levels.

```{r frontier}
plot(design)
```

## Why the number of sites matters most here

The pipeline's species-accumulation analysis (summarized in
`outputs/accum_curve_summary.csv`) shows that accumulated richness keeps rising
as sites are added, reaching about four fifths of the detected pool only near
50 sites, while species turnover between sites flattens around 25 sites.
In a two-level design with modest per-sample detection, richness is governed by
how many sites are visited, not by deeper sampling within a site, the opposite
end of the spectrum from the marine three-level survey where cheap molecular
replicates did the work.
The count goal captures this: it maximizes the number of sampled sites that
detect the target, and fixing the site count turns the problem into maximizing
detection within a single site.

```{r count-goal}
design_count <- allocate(
  theta  = theta_one,
  cost   = fresh_cost,
  goal   = "count",
  budget = 3000
)
design_count$n
```

## Designing for the assemblage

`allocate_assemblage()` sets the design by the whole target set, so the design
serves the hardest-to-detect member.

```{r assemblage}
theta_mat <- as.matrix(fresh_theta[, c("psi", "p")])
rownames(theta_mat) <- fresh_theta$species

assemblage <- allocate_assemblage(
  theta  = theta_mat,
  cost   = fresh_cost,
  budget = 3000
)
assemblage
```

## Recap

The freshwater survey is the shallow-design counterpart to the marine example:
with two levels and no cheap inner replicate to exploit, the allocation rule
offers little gain over a naive split, and richness across the harbor is
governed by the number of sites visited.
Together the two vignettes show the rule's central lesson, that the value of
optimizing effort allocation grows with the depth of the design.
The full occupancy fits, accumulation curves, and turnover analysis behind
these inputs live in `data-raw/analysis/carp/` and are reported in the
accompanying manuscript.
